meta.method: Evidence gathered via web-search result excerpts; direct page fetches to sec.gov and aboutamazon.com were blocked by the session network policy, so filings were read through search-engine excerpts rather than full documents. Items marked 'unverified' or '(secondary)' were not confirmed against a primary source.

cases.name: Amazon
cases.archetypeWhy: Entered online retail at the start of the transition and turned scale, logistics and later infrastructure into durable advantages, though it lost money for years first.
cases.positionBefore: A 1990s online bookseller with no stores; by year-end 1997 it reported 1.5 million cumulative customers and $147.8M in revenue (+838%).
cases.thesis: Management argued that market leadership, not near-term profit, would drive long-term shareholder value, and that it would invest boldly and optimise for cash flow rather than GAAP optics.

thesisQuote.text: We will continue to make investment decisions in light of long-term market leadership considerations rather than short-term profitability considerations or short-term Wall Street reactions.

cases.decision: Reinvest operating cash into customer experience, shipping subsidies and shared infrastructure ahead of profitability.
cases.immediateBenefit: Rapid customer and revenue growth that established Amazon as the default online destination.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Years of losses and dependence on capital markets; first full-year profit (2003) was small and partly attributable to an accounting change.

timeline.event: 1997 shareholder letter sets the long-term, market-leadership and cash-flow doctrine.
Agrees to run Borders.com on Amazon's platform as seller of record (after a similar Toysrus.com arrangement).
Reports first net profit: $5M on $1.12B Q4 2001 revenue.
First full-year profit: $35M net income on $5.26B revenue for 2003.
Launches Amazon Prime: unlimited two-day shipping for $79/year.
2004 letter names free cash flow per share the 'ultimate financial measure'; 2004 FCF $477M.
Launches Amazon S3, opening internal infrastructure to outside developers.
Launches Fulfillment by Amazon, renting its logistics network to third-party sellers.

cases.investments: Built: fulfillment network, Prime, marketplace, FBA and AWS infrastructure. Outsourced: last-mile carriage largely to carriers in this period (not further verified here); sold its own platform to other retailers (Borders, Toys R Us).
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That consumers would trade the in-store experience for selection, price and reliable delivery, and that convenience (e.g., flat-fee fast shipping) would increase purchase frequency.
cases.economics: Fixed-cost logistics and software were amortised over growing volume and then rented to others (FBA, AWS); 2004 fixed assets were $246M, about 4% of sales, and FCF was $477M (2003: $346M). Fortune reported a $36M accounting change accounted for the whole 2003 profit.
cases.outcome: Survived the dot-com bust, reached GAAP profitability in Q4 2001 and full-year 2003, and became the reference competitor in every later case in this set.
cases.rootCause: Success came from compounding capabilities (logistics, marketplace, infrastructure) financed by negative-working-capital retail cash flow, plus a capital-market window that funded losses; e-commerce adoption was necessary but not sufficient.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: Survivorship: many firms made similar long-term bets and failed; Amazon's financing before the 2000 crash and timing may explain as much as strategy.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: Store-based incumbents (Borders, Toys R Us) outsourced their web operations to Amazon rather than building them; pure plays like Webvan built heavy infrastructure for a single category.
cases.plausibleAlternative: A narrower, profit-first books-and-media retailer was plausible and would likely have survived, but with low confidence it would have generated AWS/FBA-scale optionality.
cases.agenticParallel: Treat agent-facing capabilities (structured catalog, real-time inventory, fulfillment promises, APIs) as compounding infrastructure that can later be offered to others, rather than a one-off channel project.
cases.similarityWhy: Agentic commerce, like early e-commerce, rewards firms whose underlying logistics, data and APIs are good enough to be exposed to machines and third parties.
evidenceFor: Amazon's later platforms (FBA, AWS) began as internal capabilities opened to outsiders, the same move as exposing commerce APIs to agents.
Prime showed that removing friction from repeat purchasing changes behavior, which is what delegated buying also targets.
evidenceAgainst: Amazon controlled the customer interface; in agentic commerce the interface may belong to a third-party AI agent.
1990s capital markets tolerated multi-year losses that may not be available today.
cases.futureConsequence: Firms that build agent-callable inventory, pricing and fulfillment now may be able to rent those capabilities to smaller merchants later.
cases.lessonTest: Can at least one capability you build for agent commerce (e.g., real-time availability API) be productised for third parties within 24 months? If not, it is a cost centre, not a compounding asset.

cases.name: Walmart
cases.archetypeWhy: An early, half-committed online venture (2000) gave way to a late, expensive catch-up (Jet.com 2016, store-based grocery pickup) that reached e-commerce profitability only in 2025.
cases.positionBefore: The largest US store-based retailer with dense store coverage and a low-price model, but a minor online presence.
cases.thesis: In 2000 it treated online as a separate, venture-style unit; by 2016 it bought talent and technology (Jet.com) to accelerate, then built e-commerce around stores as pickup and delivery nodes.

thesisQuote.text: [Walmart] acquired Jet.com for approximately $3 billion in cash, a portion of which will be paid over time, and $300 million of Walmart shares, all of which will be paid over time.
thesisQuote.who: Walmart completion press release (deal terms; a verbatim management rationale quote was not verified in this pass)

cases.decision: Acquire Jet.com (Aug 2016) and put Marc Lore in charge of US e-commerce, then lean on stores for grocery pickup and delivery.
cases.immediateBenefit: Instant e-commerce leadership talent and pricing technology, plus a fast path to scale using existing stores.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Years of e-commerce losses and a ~$3.3B brand that was shut down in 2020.

timeline.event: Forms Walmart.com as a separate Palo Alto company with Accel Partners, with its own board and management.
Buys out Accel's stake and moves toward integrating the site with store operations.
Agrees to acquire Jet.com for ~$3B cash.
Closes Jet.com: ~$3B cash plus $300M of Walmart shares; Marc Lore becomes CEO of Walmart eCommerce US.
Grocery pickup reported on track for ~3,100 stores and delivery 1,600 stores by end of FY2020.
Announces it will discontinue Jet.com.
Launches Walmart+ at $98/year (vs $119 Prime), centred on delivery from stores.
Reports first profitable e-commerce quarter (Q1 FY2026), with US online sales +21% and global ad revenue +50%.

cases.investments: Built: store-based pickup/delivery, Walmart+, advertising business. Bought: Jet.com (talent, pricing tech). Initially outsourced governance of online to a VC-backed separate entity (2000-2001).
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That shoppers, especially for grocery, would value the convenience of ordering online but receiving from a nearby store, at Walmart prices.
cases.economics: Stores already held inventory near customers, so the incremental cost of pickup was lower than building new DCs; profitability reportedly came from declining fulfillment costs plus high-margin advertising and membership income.
cases.outcome: Walmart became a leading US online grocer and reported its first profitable e-commerce quarter in May 2025, nearly 25 years after its first online venture.
cases.rootCause: Late start was partly organisational (2000 separation) and partly category (grocery requires proximity); recovery came from re-valuing existing assets (stores, supplier scale), not from the acquired brand.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: Jet.com can be read either as a $3.3B write-off or as an acqui-hire that 'still paid off' by reshaping leadership (as Axios argued); the counterfactual is unknowable.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: Amazon built dedicated fulfillment centers and a marketplace from scratch; Sears and Toys R Us had stores too but lacked capital or focus to convert them into fulfillment nodes.
cases.plausibleAlternative: Committing to store-fulfilled online grocery around 2010 instead of 2016-2019 was plausible given its assets; moderate confidence it would have shortened the loss period, low confidence on magnitude.
cases.agenticParallel: Identify which existing assets appreciate when agents do the shopping: store inventory accuracy, local fulfillment, price competitiveness and first-party customer data that agents can query.
cases.similarityWhy: Agents will route to whoever can reliably confirm availability, price and delivery time, which are asset-based capabilities incumbents already partly own.
evidenceFor: Walmart's online turnaround came from repurposing stores, mirroring how incumbents might expose existing inventory to agents.
Profitability depended on adjacent revenue (ads, membership), a model agent intermediaries may disrupt or replicate.
evidenceAgainst: Walmart owned the customer relationship via its app; agent platforms may disintermediate it.
Store density is a US-specific advantage not every retailer has.
cases.futureConsequence: Retailers with accurate, real-time local inventory may win agent-routed orders even without superior front-ends.
cases.lessonTest: Measure store-level inventory accuracy today; if it is not high enough for an agent to promise availability with confidence, that asset will not appreciate.

cases.name: Alibaba / Taobao / Alipay
cases.archetypeWhy: Launched Taobao in 2003 as a local counter to eBay's acquisition of EachNet and built trust and payments infrastructure that let it overtake eBay in China by 2006.
cases.positionBefore: A B2B marketplace (Alibaba.com) facing eBay's entry into Chinese consumer e-commerce via EachNet.
cases.thesis: Compete locally against a global incumbent by removing seller fees and solving the trust problem in an environment with weak payments and low trust between strangers.

thesisQuote.text: eBay may be the shark in the ocean, but we are the crocodile in the Yangtze River.

cases.decision: Launch Taobao with free listings and pair it with escrow-style payment (Alipay) and buyer-seller messaging.
cases.immediateBenefit: Rapid seller and buyer acquisition versus fee-charging eBay EachNet.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: No listing-fee revenue for years, requiring later monetisation via advertising and services; payment arm became a separate, regulated entity outside the listed company.

timeline.event: Taobao launched (secondary sources give May 10, 2003) in response to eBay's EachNet acquisition.
Alipay escrow payment introduced to address trust (year per brief and secondary sources; not confirmed against a primary filing in this pass).
Ma frames the contest as local 'crocodile' vs global 'shark'.
eBay announces it will fold its China site into a joint venture with Tom Online, contributing $40M for 49%.
Singles' Day GMV of RMB36.2B (US$5.8B) settled through Alipay within 24 hours (F-1).
Files F-1; describes Alipay as a related company providing payment and escrow services.

cases.investments: Built: marketplace, escrow payments, seller tools. Did not build first-party inventory or logistics in this period (logistics later via partners; not verified here).
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That Chinese consumers would buy from unknown small sellers online if payment risk was removed by a trusted escrow intermediary.
cases.economics: Free listings maximised liquidity; monetisation shifted to merchant services. SEC correspondence noted Alibaba marketplaces were ~33.9% of Alipay's payment volume in FY2014, showing payments had grown beyond the marketplace.
cases.outcome: Taobao displaced eBay in Chinese C2C; secondary sources report share shifting from 8% to 59% (Taobao) and 79% to 36% (eBay) between 2003 and 2005 (unverified against primary data). eBay folded its China site into a JV in December 2006.
cases.rootCause: Local trust infrastructure and fee strategy beat a global brand with a transplanted model; regulatory and cultural familiarity also mattered.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: eBay's own execution errors (platform migration to a US system, fee charging) may explain as much of the outcome as Alibaba's strategy.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: eBay charged listing fees and integrated EachNet into a global platform; it later handed control of its China business to a local partner.
cases.plausibleAlternative: eBay could plausibly have kept EachNet locally run and fee-free longer; low-to-moderate confidence this would have reversed the outcome given Alibaba's payments lead.
cases.agenticParallel: Agentic commerce has a trust gap (will an agent spend my money correctly?) similar to China's 2003 payment trust gap; whoever provides escrow-like guarantees, mandates and dispute resolution for agent purchases may capture the market.
cases.similarityWhy: Both transitions hinge on a trust primitive (escrow then; delegated payment authorisation now) rather than on the shopping interface itself.
evidenceFor: Alipay solved stranger-to-stranger payment risk, analogous to agent-to-merchant payment authorisation.
A free, local platform beat an incumbent's paid model, similar to open agent protocols vs closed channels.
evidenceAgainst: China in 2003 lacked card infrastructure; Western markets today have mature payments and chargebacks.
Taobao owned the consumer interface; agent platforms may be owned by AI firms, not retailers.
cases.futureConsequence: The party that controls agent payment authorisation and dispute resolution may capture platform economics regardless of who builds the agent.
cases.lessonTest: Can a customer's agent buy from you with a scoped, revocable payment mandate and a clear dispute path today? If not, trust, not discovery, is your bottleneck.

cases.name: Shopify
cases.archetypeWhy: Scaled as an enabler for independent merchants, IPO'd in 2015 and grew GMV to $292.3B in 2024; its 2019-2023 attempt to own logistics was reversed.
cases.positionBefore: A software provider for small online merchants; in 2014 it reported $105M revenue, ~$3.8B GMV and a $22.3M net loss.
cases.thesis: Give millions of independent merchants the tools large retailers have, monetising through subscriptions and, increasingly, payments and services ('merchant solutions').

thesisQuote.text: We plan on spending over $1 billion to build and operate the Shopify Fulfillment Network over the next few years.
thesisQuote.who: Craig Miller, Shopify CPO, at Unite

cases.decision: Build a fulfillment network (2019) and acquire logistics firms (6 River Systems, Deliverr), then sell the logistics business to Flexport (2023).
cases.immediateBenefit: A two-day-shipping answer to Amazon Prime for independent merchants.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Capital intensity and operational complexity outside its software core, ending in a $1.3B impairment and ~23% headcount reduction.

timeline.event: IPO on NYSE and TSX at $17, raising $131M at roughly $1.27B valuation.
Announces Shopify Fulfillment Network, planning to spend over $1B.
Agrees to sell most of its logistics business to Flexport (closed 2023-06-06) for equity; records $1.3B impairment; cuts ~23% of headcount.
GMV $292.3B, revenue $8.88B, merchant solutions $6.53B.
Announces Shopify merchants will be able to sell inside ChatGPT via OpenAI's Instant Checkout (Agentic Commerce Protocol).
Winter '26 Edition announces Agentic Storefronts on Shopify Catalog, syndicating merchants to ChatGPT, Copilot, Google AI Mode and Gemini.
Agentic Storefronts rollout in ChatGPT, with checkout on the merchant's own store as OpenAI moves Instant Checkout to Apps.

cases.investments: Built: storefront software, payments (merchant solutions), catalog and agent syndication. Attempted to build then outsourced: physical fulfillment (to Flexport).
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That brands and small merchants would sell direct to consumers across many channels rather than only through marketplaces.
cases.economics: Merchant solutions (payments, capital, shipping labels) were ~74% of 2024 revenue ($6.53B of $8.88B), so revenue scales with merchant GMV; the logistics push added fixed costs that did not fit this model.
cases.outcome: Platform model succeeded; vertical integration into logistics was reversed within four years.
cases.rootCause: Success came from aggregating fragmented merchants and taking a share of GMV; the logistics setback was a capital-model mismatch rather than an e-commerce adoption problem.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: The logistics episode may have been a reasonable option bet given 2020-2021 pandemic demand that later normalised, not a strategic error.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: Amazon owns both marketplace and logistics; Shopify ultimately partnered for logistics while keeping merchants as the brand owners.
cases.plausibleAlternative: Partnering for fulfillment from the start (as it eventually did with Flexport) was plausible; moderate confidence it would have avoided the impairment, low confidence on the effect on merchant growth.
cases.agenticParallel: Making agent-readiness (structured catalog, agent checkout, syndication to AI channels) a default setting for millions of merchants, as Shopify is attempting with Agentic Storefronts.
cases.similarityWhy: Shopify is directly replaying its enabler role in the agent channel, and its 2025-2026 changes show the channel rules are still shifting.
evidenceFor: Shopify syndicates merchants to multiple AI assistants from one admin, as it once did for web, social and marketplaces.
OpenAI's shift from native Instant Checkout to merchant-site checkout shows enablers can renegotiate where the transaction happens.
evidenceAgainst: AI platforms may prefer direct merchant integrations or their own checkout, reducing the need for an intermediary.
Agentic order volumes are not yet verified at scale; third-party claims of rapid growth are unconfirmed.
cases.futureConsequence: Small merchants may become agent-visible by default, shifting competition from discoverability to data quality and price.
cases.lessonTest: Check whether your catalog data (attributes, availability, policies) passes an AI channel's ingestion without manual fixes; if an enabler can do it for millions of small merchants, your differentiation cannot be mere presence.

cases.name: Flipkart
cases.archetypeWhy: Early and dominant domestic player whose local adaptations (cash on delivery, own logistics) won scale and a $16B Walmart deal, but which has remained loss-making and exposed to regulation.
cases.positionBefore: A small online bookseller in a market with low card penetration and weak logistics.
cases.thesis: Indian consumers would buy online only if they could pay at the door and trust delivery, so the company had to build payment and logistics workarounds itself.

thesisQuote.text: Flipkart pioneers a Cash-on-Delivery payment option, letting consumers pay for their orders in cash upon doorstep receipt of their ordered goods.
thesisQuote.who: Business Insider India (contemporaneous summary, not a management quote)

cases.decision: Offer cash on delivery (2010) and build its own logistics arm, Ekart (2010).
cases.immediateBenefit: Unlocked customers without cards and reduced fear of non-delivery.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Cash handling, returns and logistics costs that contributed to persistent losses.

timeline.event: Founded (implied by '10 years in the making' in 2018 coverage).
Introduces cash on delivery.
Launches own logistics arm, Ekart.
Walmart announces acquisition of a 77% stake for $16B, valuing Flipkart around $20-21B.
Press Note 2 (2018) FDI rules take effect, banning marketplace-mandated exclusives and treating vendors with >25% of purchases from the marketplace group as controlled inventory.
Flipkart Internet reports a loss of INR 4,845.7 Cr, up from INR 3,404.3 Cr in FY2022.
PhonePe (acquired by Flipkart in 2015/2016; sources differ; later separated) reports Rs 630 Cr adjusted PAT on Rs 7,115 Cr revenue.

cases.investments: Built: COD capability, Ekart logistics, payments (PhonePe, later separated). Outsourced little in the early phase because local infrastructure did not exist.
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That Indian consumers would shift online if payment risk moved to the retailer (COD) and delivery reliability was demonstrated.
cases.economics: Growth was funded by venture and later strategic capital; losses persisted (e.g., INR 4,845.7 Cr at Flipkart Internet in FY2023), and FDI rules constrained inventory-led margin strategies.
cases.outcome: Became a leading Indian e-commerce platform and sold control to Walmart in 2018; profitability remains unproven at the group level based on sources found.
cases.rootCause: E-commerce adoption required local infrastructure that Flipkart built itself; profitability was then shaped by competition with Amazon, capital-funded discounting and FDI regulation rather than by adoption.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: The $16B exit can be seen as a financial success driven by a strategic bidding contest (Walmart vs Amazon) rather than by proven unit economics.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: Amazon India entered later with global capital and similar COD and logistics adaptations; regulation affected both.
cases.plausibleAlternative: Relying on third-party couriers and prepaid payments only was possible but, with moderate confidence, would have limited reach in 2010-era India.
cases.agenticParallel: Where agent payment and identity rails are immature (as card rails were in 2010 India), retailers may need to build their own agent-compatible payment and fulfillment guarantees rather than wait for the ecosystem.
cases.similarityWhy: The infrastructure-gap logic transfers, but agentic commerce is emerging in markets that already have digital payments.
evidenceFor: COD shows that shifting risk away from the consumer can unlock adoption, as agent purchase guarantees may need to.
Regulatory rules (Press Note 2) reshaped e-commerce economics, as agent-commerce rules may.
evidenceAgainst: India's UPI-era payment rails now differ greatly from 2010.
Flipkart's challenge was physical access; agentic commerce's challenge is delegation and trust.
cases.futureConsequence: Markets with weak agent-trust infrastructure may favour vertically integrated players that absorb delegation risk themselves.
cases.lessonTest: Identify the single risk that stops customers delegating a purchase to an agent (wrong item, unauthorised spend, returns) and test whether absorbing it yourself, COD-style, lifts conversion.

cases.name: Mercado Libre
cases.archetypeWhy: An early regional marketplace that allied with eBay instead of being displaced, then built payments (Mercado Pago) and logistics (Mercado Envios) itself, reaching $21B revenue and $1.9B net income in 2024.
cases.positionBefore: A late-1990s Latin American online marketplace operating in markets with low banking penetration and fragmented logistics.
cases.thesis: Own the missing infrastructure layers (payments, then shipping) so the marketplace can work in markets where they are weak, completing an e-commerce 'suite'.

thesisQuote.text: During 2013, we launched the MercadoEnvios shipping solution in Brazil and Argentina [described as the last piece of our e-commerce suite].

cases.decision: Build in-house payments (Mercado Pago, 2003 per secondary source) and an integrated shipping solution (Mercado Envios, 2013) instead of relying on banks and carriers.
cases.immediateBenefit: Higher conversion and trust on the marketplace and a uniform delivery experience for buyers.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Credit risk and capital needs from becoming a lender (credit portfolio $6.6B at end-2024) and heavy logistics investment.

timeline.event: Strategic alliance with eBay, which becomes a stockholder; non-compete later expires 2006-09-24.
Mercado Pago launched as an on-site payment solution (secondary source).
IPO on Nasdaq (~$333M deal value per database source).
Launches MercadoEnvios in Brazil and Argentina; >5% of combined items shipped through it in Q4 2013 (earnings call, as excerpted in search).
Net revenue ~$21B (+38% USD), commerce $12.2B, fintech $8.6B, GMV $51.5B, net income $1.9B; Mercado Envios handled 1.8B items, 49% same/next day.

cases.investments: Built: payments, credit, shipping and fulfillment. Partnered: eBay alliance (2001) and carriers integrated into Mercado Envios.
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That consumers would buy online at scale if payment and delivery reliability were guaranteed by the platform.
cases.economics: Fintech and logistics raised take rates and lock-in; 2024 operating margin was 12.7% and the credit book grew 74% to $6.6B, showing revenue diversification with added risk.
cases.outcome: Became Latin America's leading e-commerce and fintech platform by revenue reported in its filings.
cases.rootCause: Success rested on vertically integrating infrastructure the region lacked, plus a partnership that neutralised the global incumbent; macro and FX volatility remain major risk factors (FX-neutral growth 101% vs 38% in USD in 2024).
cases.alternativeInterpretation: eBay's decision to partner rather than compete (as it did in China) may have been as decisive as Mercado Libre's own strategy.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: eBay competed directly in China and lost; in Latin America it took a stake and stayed out.
cases.plausibleAlternative: Remaining an asset-light marketplace was possible; low confidence it would have achieved comparable trust or margins given regional infrastructure gaps.
cases.agenticParallel: Retailers and platforms may need to own the agent-facing trust and settlement layers (identity, payment mandate, delivery promise) where the ecosystem does not yet supply them.
cases.similarityWhy: The infrastructure-ownership logic transfers, but MELI's gaps were physical and financial while agentic gaps are mostly protocol and trust.
evidenceFor: Mercado Pago grew into a business beyond the marketplace, as agent payment layers might.
Integrated delivery promises (49% same/next day) are exactly what agents need to compare options.
evidenceAgainst: Agentic protocols are being standardised by large AI and payments firms, reducing the need for each retailer to build its own.
MELI's lending risk has no clear analogue in agent commerce.
cases.futureConsequence: Platforms that already control payment and delivery data can offer agents reliable promises sooner than those that rely on partners.
cases.lessonTest: Can you return a machine-readable, guaranteed delivery date and total landed price for every SKU within one API call? If not, you are dependent on someone else's infrastructure for agent orders.

cases.name: eBay
cases.archetypeWhy: An early winner in online auctions that bought PayPal and expanded globally, but lost China, shifted from auctions to fixed price under pressure and later separated PayPal.
cases.positionBefore: A 1995-era person-to-person auction site for collectibles; IPO in September 1998 at $18 per share.
cases.thesis: A neutral marketplace connecting individual buyers and sellers, with network effects from listings and feedback, later extended with payments (PayPal) and communications (Skype).

thesisQuote.text: unverified: a primary-source eBay thesis quote from 1998 filings could not be retrieved in this pass.

cases.decision: Acquire PayPal (announced July 2002, $1.5B) and Skype (2005, ~$2.6B up front) to extend the marketplace into adjacent infrastructure.
cases.immediateBenefit: PayPal reduced payment friction on eBay; Skype was pitched as a buyer-seller communication tool.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Skype did not fit and was sold in 2009; PayPal became more valuable outside eBay and was spun off in 2015 after activist pressure.

timeline.event: IPO at $18 per share; opens at $53.50; ~$63M raised; Omidyar owns ~42%.
Announces acquisition of PayPal for $1.5B.
Agrees to buy Skype for ~$2.6B in cash and stock plus potential earn-out.
Announces China JV with Tom Online, effectively exiting direct operation in China.
Fee changes favouring fixed-price listings take effect under incoming CEO John Donahoe; seller feedback restrictions follow in May, prompting a seller boycott.
Completes separation of PayPal after activist Carl Icahn's campaign.

cases.investments: Built: marketplace, feedback/trust system. Bought: PayPal, Skype. Did not build first-party logistics in the period covered.
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That individuals would trade with strangers online if reputation (feedback) and payment tools reduced risk, and that auctions would remain a dominant format.
cases.economics: Asset-light take-rate model; acquisitions such as Skype (~$2.6B plus up to $1.5B earn-out) diverted capital away from the core marketplace experience.
cases.outcome: Remained a large marketplace but lost relative position to Amazon in fixed-price retail and to Taobao in China; PayPal's value was realised outside eBay.
cases.rootCause: Consumer preference shifted from auctions to fixed price and fast delivery, which favoured inventory/logistics owners; acquisition choices and China execution were management factors separate from e-commerce adoption.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: eBay's decline in relative share may simply reflect market expansion beyond collectibles into categories where it never had an advantage, rather than strategic error.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: Amazon invested in fulfillment and Prime; Taobao offered free listings and escrow in China.
cases.plausibleAlternative: Investing earlier in fulfillment services or seller logistics, as Amazon did with FBA in 2006, was plausible; low confidence it would have fit eBay's asset-light culture.
cases.agenticParallel: Formats optimised for human engagement (auctions, browsing) may lose share when agents buy on fixed criteria; marketplaces must decide whether to standardise listings for machine comparison.
cases.similarityWhy: The auction-to-fixed-price shift resembles a shift to agent-friendly structured offers, but eBay's losses also had acquisition and geography causes.
evidenceFor: eBay had to reprice and re-rank to favour fixed price, much as agent channels reward structured, comparable offers.
Trust systems (feedback) were core; agent commerce needs machine-readable trust signals.
evidenceAgainst: Agents may handle negotiation and auctions well, reversing rather than repeating the format shift.
eBay's China loss was mainly competitive and local, not format-related.
cases.futureConsequence: Marketplaces with unstructured, idiosyncratic listings may be under-represented in agent recommendations.
cases.lessonTest: What share of your listings have complete, normalised attributes and fixed prices an agent can compare? Track agent-referred conversion by listing completeness.

cases.name: Best Buy
cases.archetypeWhy: A store-based electronics retailer that outlasted Circuit City and adapted to online price competition rather than dying from showrooming; adaptation details are largely unverified in this pass.
cases.positionBefore: Per the Richmond Fed, Best Buy overtook Circuit City with central checkout, self-service floors and low-margin traffic-driving products (peripherals, games, CDs).
cases.thesis: unverified in this pass: the 'Renew Blue' turnaround (announced 2012 under Hubert Joly) reportedly combined online price matching, using stores to ship online orders and vendor partnerships; no primary source could be retrieved.

thesisQuote.text: unverified: Renew Blue primary-source quote could not be retrieved in this pass.

cases.decision: Match online prices and turn stores into fulfillment and showroom assets rather than fighting showrooming (unverified details; see thesis).
cases.immediateBenefit: Reduced the incentive for customers to see products in store and buy elsewhere (unverified).
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Price matching compresses gross margin, requiring cost cuts and vendor funding to offset (reasoned, not verified with figures).

timeline.event: Overtakes Circuit City with better locations and a self-service, central-checkout format.
Main specialist rival Circuit City announces liquidation, leaving Best Buy as the largest US electronics specialist.

cases.investments: Reportedly kept and repurposed its store fleet as fulfillment and showroom assets (unverified in this pass).
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That shoppers would still value hands-on demonstration, advice and immediate pickup if price was no longer a reason to defect (unverified).
cases.economics: unverified: no Best Buy financial figures could be confirmed in this research pass; omit numbers until sourced.
cases.outcome: Best Buy survived the period in which Circuit City liquidated (2009); later outcome figures not verified here.
cases.rootCause: Survival compared with Circuit City reflects earlier format advantages documented by the Richmond Fed; the specific contribution of Renew Blue is unverified here.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: Best Buy may have benefited mainly from consolidation (Circuit City's exit) and vendor desire for physical showrooms, rather than from its own e-commerce adaptations.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: Circuit City cut experienced staff and liquidated; Amazon competed purely on price and selection online.
cases.plausibleAlternative: A store-shrinking, online-first strategy was plausible; low confidence about outcome without verified data.
cases.agenticParallel: Price-matching an AI agent's best-found price and making local stock available for immediate agent-booked pickup, so stores become fulfillment nodes rather than showrooms for others.
cases.similarityWhy: Showrooming is the closest historical analogue to agents comparing prices across retailers, but the Best Buy adaptation evidence here is unverified.
evidenceFor: Agents will compare prices instantly, intensifying the showrooming pressure Best Buy faced.
Physical proximity still matters for same-day fulfillment of agent orders.
evidenceAgainst: Agents may not value in-store advice, removing Best Buy's service differentiation.
Key Best Buy figures and dates are unverified in this dataset.
cases.futureConsequence: Retailers may need explicit policies for matching agent-discovered prices.
cases.lessonTest: Run a controlled test: match the lowest agent-surfaced price for in-stock items with same-day pickup and measure margin loss vs order retention.

cases.name: Webvan
cases.archetypeWhy: Built highly automated grocery infrastructure ahead of demonstrated demand and filed for bankruptcy in July 2001, about 20 months after its November 1999 IPO.
cases.positionBefore: A venture-backed start-up founded by Louis Borders (Borders bookstores co-founder) with no stores, entering low-margin grocery.
cases.thesis: Automated distribution centers plus a web store would make home grocery delivery cheaper than supermarkets at high volume.

thesisQuote.text: Our interactive Webstore and highly automated distribution center were designed to operate efficiently at high volumes.

cases.decision: Commit ~$1B with Bechtel to build 26 automated distribution centers before proving demand in its first market.
cases.immediateBenefit: A credible story of scale and cost leadership that supported a $375M IPO.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Fixed costs that required volumes the prospectus itself said would take 'several years' to reach.

timeline.event: Announces ~$1B deal with Bechtel to build 26 distribution centers.
Prospectus: first DC designed for volume equal to ~18 supermarkets; warns DCs will not run at designed capacity for several years.
IPO raises $375M at $15; closes first day up 66%.
Completes merger with HomeGrocer; purchase price ~$1,044M in stock.
FY2000 10-K reports accumulated deficit of $612.7M and substantial doubt about going concern.
Files Chapter 11, shuts operations, ~2,000 employees laid off (date per secondary sources; some say June).

cases.investments: Built: proprietary automated DCs (~330,000-350,000 sq ft each per secondary sources), delivery fleet and software. Outsourced: DC construction to Bechtel.
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That households would shift a large share of weekly grocery shopping online quickly enough to fill very large DCs.
cases.economics: Each DC was a large fixed asset (Bechtel's $1B for 26 sites implies ~$38M each; '$30M+' and '$35M' figures appear only in secondary sources). With an accumulated deficit of $612.7M by end-2000 and DCs below capacity, unit costs stayed high.
cases.outcome: Bankrupt in July 2001 after losing an estimated ~$830M (per SF Chronicle headline cited by secondary sources).
cases.rootCause: Capital structure and sequencing (build for scale before demand) were decisive; grocery's thin margins and the 2000-2001 funding collapse removed time to reach utilisation. The idea of online grocery itself was later validated by others.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: Webvan may have been killed mainly by the closing of capital markets in 2000-2001; with patient funding its utilisation curve might have worked.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: Tesco picked orders from existing stores, using sunk assets, which Wharton contrasted with Webvan's greenfield DCs.
cases.plausibleAlternative: Store-pick or a single-market DC proven to profitability before expansion was plausible; moderate confidence it would have survived, lower confidence it would have reached national scale.
cases.agenticParallel: Building expensive autonomous-checkout or agent-specific infrastructure ahead of demonstrated agent order volume, instead of exposing existing systems to agents first.
cases.similarityWhy: The core risk is identical: fixed investment sized for an adoption curve that has not yet been observed.
evidenceFor: Agentic order volumes are not yet reliably measured; third-party growth claims are unverified.
Webvan's own prospectus disclosed slow ramp risk, as current agent forecasts carry wide uncertainty.
evidenceAgainst: Agent-readiness is mostly software and data, far cheaper and more reversible than warehouses.
Capital markets today are not in a 2000-2001-style collapse (as of sources reviewed).
cases.futureConsequence: Firms that over-build agent infrastructure may carry stranded costs if AI platforms change protocols (as OpenAI's Instant Checkout shift showed).
cases.lessonTest: Before funding agent-specific infrastructure, require observed agent-originated orders in one category/market to hit a pre-set utilisation threshold; stage spending accordingly.

cases.name: Pets.com
cases.archetypeWhy: Spent heavily on brand advertising to acquire customers for low-margin, bulky pet supplies sold below cost, and announced its wind-down about nine months after its February 2000 IPO.
cases.positionBefore: A 1999 start-up (inception February 17, 1999) with no stores in a category dominated by pet superstores and grocers.
cases.thesis: Become the leading online pet-supply brand by acquiring customers quickly through mass marketing and expecting scale to fix margins.

thesisQuote.text: unverified: a verbatim thesis quote from the S-1 could not be retrieved; S-1 financial tables were confirmed via search excerpts.

cases.decision: Spend on national brand advertising (including a Super Bowl spot) while selling at negative gross margin.
cases.immediateBenefit: High brand awareness (the sock puppet) and an $82.5M IPO in February 2000.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Every sale lost money before marketing; growth increased losses.

timeline.event: Inception.
S-1 shows $619K net sales from inception to Sept 30, 1999, negative gross margin of $1,223K and $11,815K marketing and sales expense.
Super Bowl XXXIV ad (cost widely cited as ~$1.2M; secondary).
IPO on Nasdaq at $11, raising $82.5M.
FY2000 10-K reports a 1999 net loss of about $61.8M.
Announces wind-down; lays off 255 of 320 employees.

cases.investments: Built: brand, website, distribution. Heavy external spend on advertising agencies and media.
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That pet owners would switch routine, heavy, low-value purchases online despite shipping costs.
cases.economics: From inception to Sept 30, 1999, marketing and sales spend ($11.8M) was ~19x net sales ($0.62M) and gross margin was negative (-$1.2M), so customer acquisition could not be recovered.
cases.outcome: Liquidated in November 2000; stock fell from $11 to about $0.19 (secondary).
cases.rootCause: Category economics (bulky, low-margin goods with high shipping cost) and negative gross margin were primary; the 2000 capital-market reversal removed runway. E-commerce adoption was not the main cause, as online pet retail later succeeded.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: Pets.com may have been simply too early: later online pet retailers succeeded with subscriptions and denser logistics, suggesting timing and infrastructure rather than concept failed.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: Store-based pet superstores kept bulky-goods economics in stores (competitor details not further verified here).
cases.plausibleAlternative: Focusing on positive-gross-margin items or subscription replenishment before mass advertising was plausible; moderate confidence it would have extended runway.
cases.agenticParallel: Paying heavily for placement or visibility in AI agent channels (sponsored answers, agent marketing) for products whose unit economics are negative.
cases.similarityWhy: Customer acquisition cost versus contribution margin transfers directly, but agent channels may reduce rather than raise acquisition costs.
evidenceFor: Agent channels may introduce pay-for-placement economics that, like 1999 advertising, can mask negative contribution margins.
Replenishment categories (pet food) are prime candidates for agent delegation.
evidenceAgainst: Agents could lower shipping and acquisition costs through automated replenishment, the opposite of 1999 conditions.
Pets.com's failure was mostly gross-margin math, independent of channel.
cases.futureConsequence: Retailers chasing agent visibility in replenishment categories may repeat negative-margin growth if agent fees are not priced into contribution margin.
cases.lessonTest: Compute contribution margin per agent-originated order after any agent/platform fees and fulfillment; do not scale agent marketing until it is positive.

cases.name: Borders
cases.archetypeWhy: Outsourced its online store to Amazon in 2001, relaunched its own site only in 2008, and filed for Chapter 11 in February 2011 before liquidating.
cases.positionBefore: A leading US book superstore chain with a loss-making Borders.com and international expansion.
cases.thesis: Online bookselling was a cost centre; letting Amazon run Borders.com would stop losses and let management concentrate on stores.

thesisQuote.text: The internet needs to be transferred to help in-store economics.
thesisQuote.who: Greg Josefowicz, Borders CEO (as reported in April 2001 coverage)

cases.decision: Hand Borders.com to Amazon, which became seller of record and handled inventory, fulfillment, content and customer service.
cases.immediateBenefit: Eliminated Borders.com losses (reported ~$18M+ on ~$27M sales in the year before the deal) and ~70 online jobs.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Gave its online customers, data and digital capability to its fastest-growing competitor for seven years.

timeline.event: Announces Amazon will run Borders.com as co-branded site; Amazon is seller of record; 70 Borders.com jobs cut.
Co-branded Borders.com goes live on Amazon's platform.
Announces it will retake its website and sell or franchise most of 73 overseas stores.
Relaunches its own Borders.com, ending the Amazon arrangement.
Files Chapter 11 in SDNY listing $1.27B assets and $1.29B liabilities; begins closing ~200 stores (other sources: 226).
Chapter 11 later converted to Chapter 7 liquidation (secondary; month not verified).

cases.investments: Built: store fleet and international superstores. Outsourced: entire e-commerce operation to Amazon (2001-2008).
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That book buying would remain predominantly in-store and that online would be a marginal, unprofitable channel.
cases.economics: Pre-deal Borders.com reportedly lost >$18M on ~$27M sales (fiscal period as reported); Borders later posted five straight years of losses totalling more than $900M before bankruptcy, per 2011 coverage.
cases.outcome: Bankrupt in 2011 and liquidated; Barnes & Noble acquired its trademarks and customer list (secondary).
cases.rootCause: E-commerce outsourcing removed learning and customer data; separately, debt-funded expansion, international stores, heavy music/DVD exposure and the 2008 recession weakened finances. Retrospective coverage singles out the Amazon deal as the first error.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: The 2001 deal was rational given dot-com losses; Borders' fatal problems may have been leverage, store overcapacity and the later e-book shift, which an in-house website would not have fixed.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: Barnes & Noble kept its own website (BN.com) during this period (not verified here).
cases.plausibleAlternative: Keeping a minimal in-house site to retain customer data and skills was plausible; low-to-moderate confidence it would have prevented bankruptcy.
cases.agenticParallel: Outsourcing product discovery and customer interaction to an external AI agent platform to save cost, giving the platform the customer relationship and data.
cases.similarityWhy: The decision structure is the same: cut channel cost now by letting a platform own discovery and the customer, at the risk of long-run dependence.
evidenceFor: Agent platforms may become the 'seller of record' interface while retailers only fulfil, mirroring Amazon running Borders.com.
Retailers that do not learn agent channel operations may face expensive re-entry, as Borders did in 2008.
evidenceAgainst: Agent platforms are not (yet) direct retail competitors in the way Amazon was to Borders.
Some agent integrations keep checkout on the merchant's site, preserving data (e.g., Shopify Agentic Storefronts).
cases.futureConsequence: Retailers that let agents own all customer interaction may lose the data needed to personalise or price later.
cases.lessonTest: In any agent-platform contract, confirm you retain customer identity, order data and the ability to contact the customer; if not, treat it as a Borders-type trade.

cases.name: Toys "R" Us
cases.archetypeWhy: After a failed 1999 holiday online season it outsourced e-commerce to Amazon (2000), litigated its way out (2004-2009) and, burdened by LBO debt, liquidated US operations in 2018.
cases.positionBefore: The dominant US toy specialist chain whose own site (Toysrus.com) suffered delivery failures in the 1999 holiday season.
cases.thesis: Partnering with Amazon for fulfillment and customer service would fix the operational failures of 1999 while securing exclusive toy-category status on Amazon.

thesisQuote.text: unverified: no verbatim 2000 management quote retrieved; CFO.com framed the deal as addressing fulfillment and customer service, the main factors in Toysrus.com's 1999 holiday problems.

cases.decision: Sign a 10-year exclusive alliance (Aug 2000) under which Amazon ran the site and fulfillment and Toys R Us paid Amazon a fee plus a share of sales.
cases.immediateBenefit: Reliable fulfillment and access to Amazon's traffic without building its own capability.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Dependence on a platform that later let other toy sellers in; Toys R Us lost years of in-house e-commerce learning.

timeline.event: Toysrus.com agrees to a $350,000 FTC civil penalty over 1999 holiday shipping-promise violations.
Announces 10-year alliance with Amazon; reported terms $50M/year plus a percentage of sales (press reports, not audited contract terms).
Sues Amazon for breaching exclusivity; Amazon countersues seeking $750M.
Bain, KKR and Vornado announce $6.6B LBO, leaving ~$5B of long-term debt.
NJ trial court terminates the Amazon agreement, finding Amazon breached exclusivity but awarding no damages.
After appeal (2009-03-24) and settlement (2009-06-11), Amazon pays Toys R Us $51M.
Files Chapter 11 with ~$5B+ debt; Reuters reports ~$400M/year interest payments.
US liquidation sales begin; last US stores close in late June 2018.

cases.investments: Outsourced: e-commerce operations to Amazon (2000-2006). Later had to rebuild its own site; also bore heavy LBO debt service.
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That toy buyers would shop online through the dominant online retailer but still prefer a specialist assortment it could control via exclusivity.
cases.economics: Reported payments of $50M/year to Amazon plus a share of sales (press-reported). After 2005, interest expense was $451M (FY2014) and $429M (FY2015), consuming cash that could have funded stores and digital.
cases.outcome: Chapter 11 in September 2017 and US liquidation in 2018.
cases.rootCause: LBO debt (~$400M+ annual interest) was the primary constraint; competition from Amazon and Walmart and an under-developed online business compounded it. The Amazon outsourcing is a contributing, not sole, cause.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: Without the 2005 LBO, Toys R Us might have survived as a smaller omnichannel retailer, implying financing, not e-commerce, was decisive.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: Walmart and Target used general-merchandise scale and later built their own e-commerce; Amazon opened toys to many sellers.
cases.plausibleAlternative: Rebuilding Toysrus.com in-house after 1999 with partner logistics (rather than full outsourcing) was plausible; low confidence it offsets the LBO debt burden.
cases.agenticParallel: Signing an exclusive or preferred-partner deal with one AI agent platform, paying for guaranteed placement that the platform may not be able (or willing) to honour as it scales.
cases.similarityWhy: The platform-exclusivity risk transfers strongly, but Toys R Us's failure was dominated by LBO debt, unrelated to channel strategy.
evidenceFor: Platforms have incentives to broaden supply, as Amazon did despite exclusivity, which agent platforms may also do.
Litigation to enforce exclusivity took ~5 years, longer than platform cycles.
evidenceAgainst: Agent platforms currently tend to aggregate many merchants by default, so exclusivity deals may be rare.
The decisive cause of failure was financial leverage.
cases.futureConsequence: Retailers that pay for preferred status with one agent platform may find the advantage eroded while their own capabilities atrophy.
cases.lessonTest: For any preferred-placement agent deal, check whether the counterparty can unilaterally change ranking rules, and keep a direct, agent-readable channel that works without the partner.

cases.name: Circuit City
cases.archetypeWhy: Lost its lead to Best Buy in stores before the online shift peaked, cut experienced staff in 2007 to save cost and liquidated in 2009.
cases.positionBefore: Once the leading US electronics chain; by 2000 many stores were out of date and poorly located versus newer Best Buy stores (Richmond Fed).
cases.thesis: Cost cutting would restore competitiveness against lower-price rivals; in 2007 it replaced higher-paid store staff with lower-cost hires.

thesisQuote.text: well above the market-based salary range for their role

cases.decision: Lay off ~3,400 higher-paid store associates and rehire at market rates.
cases.immediateBenefit: Lower payroll costs in the short term.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Loss of experienced sales staff, the main service advantage stores held over online sellers.

timeline.event: Announces exit from major appliances.
Best Buy overtakes it with better locations, self-service format and traffic-driving low-margin categories.
Announces ~3,400 store layoffs of associates paid above 'market-based' range, to be replaced by lower-paid hires.
Files Chapter 11 in the Eastern District of Virginia.
Announces liquidation of its 567 US stores after failing to find a buyer; ~30,000-34,000 jobs (sources differ).

cases.investments: Cut: staffing and appliances. Store refresh lagged (per Richmond Fed); online capability not verified here.
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That shoppers would choose primarily on price, so service labour was a cost to cut rather than a differentiator.
cases.economics: Payroll savings were intended to restore margins under price pressure; quantified savings were not disclosed (a spokesman declined to give wages).
cases.outcome: Bankruptcy in November 2008 and liquidation in early 2009 during the financial crisis.
cases.rootCause: Format and location disadvantages versus Best Buy (pre-dating e-commerce), management decisions (2007 layoffs, appliance exit) and the 2008 credit crisis that cut off financing; online price competition intensified but was not the sole cause.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: Former CEO Alan Wurtzel attributes the fall to leadership failures in three stages and inattention to Best Buy, implying management, not e-commerce, was decisive.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: Best Buy invested earlier in store format and traffic-driving categories and survived the 2008-2009 downturn.
cases.plausibleAlternative: Investing in service and store-fulfilled online orders rather than cutting experienced staff was plausible; low confidence it would have survived the 2008 credit freeze.
cases.agenticParallel: Cutting the human expertise (advisors, service staff) that differentiates physical retail because agents will compare price, leaving nothing an agent would prefer you for.
cases.similarityWhy: The trade-off between cost and differentiators under channel price pressure transfers, but Circuit City's collapse was heavily driven by the 2008 crisis.
evidenceFor: Agent comparison will intensify price pressure, tempting cost cuts.
If agents can't observe service quality, retailers may underinvest in it, as Circuit City did.
evidenceAgainst: Agents may bypass in-store service entirely, making the staff trade-off less relevant.
Macro credit conditions in 2008 have no current analogue verified here.
cases.futureConsequence: Retailers may need to make service quality machine-readable (warranties, installation, returns) so agents can value it.
cases.lessonTest: List which of your differentiators an agent can see and score; for those it cannot, test whether exposing them as structured data changes agent recommendations before cutting their cost.

cases.name: Sears / Sears Holdings (incl. Kmart)
cases.archetypeWhy: Combined two declining store chains in 2005, pursued a membership-led 'integrated retail' strategy while monetising real estate, and filed for Chapter 11 in 2018.
cases.positionBefore: Sears (historic catalog pioneer) and Kmart were merged by Eddie Lampert in a deal announced in November 2004 at $11B; ~3,500 stores at the 2005 merger.
cases.thesis: Transform into an 'integrated retail' company where the Shop Your Way membership links online, mobile and stores, while extracting value from real estate.

thesisQuote.text: [transforming Sears Holdings into] a truly integrated retail company

cases.decision: Prioritise Shop Your Way membership and sell 235 stores to Seritage in a $2.7B sale-leaseback (2015) rather than reinvest heavily in stores.
cases.immediateBenefit: Cash to fund operations and a member base that accounted for 69% of 2013 sales.
cases.hiddenTradeoff: Rent on former owned stores and continued under-investment in the store experience, while losses persisted.

timeline.event: Kmart announces purchase of Sears for $11B, led by Eddie Lampert.
Merger forms Sears Holdings with ~3,500 stores.
Shop Your Way wins a channel-integration award; membership becomes core of strategy.
Lampert letter: Shop Your Way members were 69% of 2013 sales (59% in 2012).
Completes Seritage sale-leaseback of 235 stores plus JV interests; $2.7B gross proceeds.
FY2016 revenue $22.14B (-12%), net loss $2.22B; going-concern doubt disclosed.
Files Chapter 11 with ~700 stores; Lampert steps down as CEO.

cases.investments: Built: Shop Your Way loyalty/membership and online/mobile platforms. Monetised rather than reinvested: real estate (Seritage).
cases.anticipatedBehavior: That rewards and personalisation would keep customers loyal across channels even as store experience lagged.
cases.economics: Real-estate sales provided liquidity ($2.7B from Seritage) while operations lost money ($2.22B net loss in FY2016); shareholder litigation alleged the Seritage deal undervalued assets (allegation, not finding).
cases.outcome: Chapter 11 in October 2018; ESL-affiliated Transformco acquired 425 stores for $5.2B in Feb 2019 (secondary).
cases.rootCause: Ownership and capital-allocation choices (real-estate monetisation, under-investment) and competition from Walmart, Home Depot and Amazon were primary; e-commerce was one pressure among several, and Sears had digital assets it did not translate into advantage.
cases.alternativeInterpretation: Sears may have been in structural decline before e-commerce, and Lampert's strategy may have maximised recovery value for investors rather than aiming to save the retailer.
cases.competitorsDidDifferently: Walmart reinvested in stores as fulfillment nodes and price; Best Buy kept stores relevant via adaptation.
cases.plausibleAlternative: Using the store base as local fulfillment for online orders (as Walmart later did) was plausible; low confidence given Sears' cash constraints.
cases.agenticParallel: Relying on a loyalty/membership programme to keep customers when agents may shop across retailers on their behalf, ignoring that agents optimise on price and availability, not points.
cases.similarityWhy: Loyalty-led defence against a channel shift is directly analogous, but Sears' failure had large financing and governance components.
evidenceFor: Agents may route around loyalty programmes unless benefits are machine-readable and material.
Sears had digital assets but did not turn them into operating advantage, a risk for retailers adding agent features superficially.
evidenceAgainst: Agents could amplify loyalty if they are instructed to use member benefits.
Sears' real-estate and governance issues are idiosyncratic.
cases.futureConsequence: Loyalty value will depend on whether agents can read and redeem it automatically.
cases.lessonTest: Test whether a customer's agent can see and apply member pricing/benefits at checkout; if not, loyalty will not defend share in delegated purchases.
